input_signals.name: GrossProfitVsWorkingCapitalPressure
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(wcap, 1), dp), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross profitability is a clean top-line measure of business quality, but it is only credible when it is not being manufactured by expanding working capital; industry-adjusted gross profit combined with low working-capital accrual pressure identifies genuinely efficient franchises.
input_signals.reasoning: Using gross profit avoids contamination from the same accrual items that appear in the accrual leg, making the two channels economically independent inputs rather than mechanical mirror images. Industry ranking of gross profitability handles the large cross-industry dispersion in cost structure, while the balance-sheet accrual leg captures receivable/inventory-financed sales growth.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( delta( wcap, 1 ), dp ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ProfitPremiumWeightedByAccrualQuality
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oiadp, at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accrual quality is not a separate return driver but a credibility weight on profitability: the profitability premium should be strongly positive among clean-accrual firms and attenuate toward zero among accrual-financed firms, whose reported profitability conveys no information.
input_signals.reasoning: The centered profitability z-score multiplied by a bounded [0,1] quality weight implements regime-dependent pricing continuously — accrual-heavy firms collapse toward zero regardless of profitability, with no point mass and no masking artifact — which is exactly the conditional structure the earlier indicator gate failed to deliver. Paired with signal 4 on identical legs, it tells us whether the interaction is best expressed as a conjunction or as an attenuation of the profitability slope.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_zscore( ratio( oiadp, at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ChronicAccrualRelianceOnProfits
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, at)), RANK(NEG(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at), 0), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The frequency, not the size, of accrual reliance is what distinguishes benign working-capital timing from systematic earnings support: a profitable firm that posts income-increasing accruals in nearly every one of the last five years is running a chronic recognition policy whose reversal is inevitable, whereas a firm with one large accrual year is usually just lumpy.
input_signals.reasoning: Counting positive-accrual years converts the accrual leg into a persistence statistic that is unit-free and immune to the negative-denominator and outlier problems that sank the GROWTH-based construction, so the ranking is stable across retailers, subscription firms, and asset-light businesses. The count is nearly uncorrelated with the magnitude-based accrual factor exposure embedded in the archive, so the profitability interaction is being tested against a genuinely different accrual construct rather than a rescaling of it.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( oibdp, at ) ), rank( neg( ts_sum( indicator( ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ), 0 ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: GrossProfitXReceivableInventoryRelease
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(ADD(recch, invch), NEG(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1))), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The asset side of the operating cycle carries the earnings-quality information: profitable firms that collect receivables and turn inventory into cash have realized sales, whereas equally profitable firms whose margins are accompanied by receivable and inventory build are recognizing revenue that has not been collected.
input_signals.reasoning: Paired with signal 1, this isolates exactly which half of the operating cycle produced the archive's strongest alpha — an identical profitability leg and scaling, with only the accrual component swapped, so the comparison is clean. Note that generation 0 tested this component against a *margin-change* profitability leg and found nothing, so this also tells us whether the profitability leg must be a level rather than a change for the interaction to fire.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), rank( ratio( coalesce( add( recch, invch ), neg( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ) ) ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: PersistentCashCycleReleaseWithProfit
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(oibdp, at), 3)), RANK(TS_SUM(RATIO(COALESCE(ADD(apalch, ADD(recch, invch)), NEG(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1))), at), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A single year of working-capital release can be liquidation or a demand shock, but five years of cumulative release alongside sustained operating profitability identifies a structurally cash-generative operating model whose reported profits require no incremental working-capital investment to sustain.
input_signals.reasoning: Cumulating the working-capital cash flow over five years averages out the mean-reverting timing noise that makes one-year accrual measures fragile, while smoothing profitability over three years ensures the interaction conditions on a persistent profit state rather than a single strong year. If the five-year version dominates the one-year version in FF5 alpha, the mechanism is a durable business-model attribute; if it is weaker, the archive's result is a short-horizon cash-timing effect and future refinements should stay at annual frequency.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( ratio( oibdp, at ), 3 ) ), rank( ts_sum( ratio( coalesce( add( apalch, add( recch, invch ) ), neg( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ) ), at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: SupplyChainPowerVsPaymentStretch
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), RANK(MIN(RATIO(apalch, at), RATIO(invch, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Extending payables is a sign of bargaining power only when inventory is simultaneously being converted to cash; a profitable firm that stretches suppliers while inventory piles up is delaying payment because goods are not selling, and that state reverses.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than re-running the generation-0 aggregate working-capital test that already produced a null alpha, this conditions the proven payables leg on the inventory leg through a weakest-link MIN, which separates genuine supply-chain power from distress-driven payment stretching — two states the additive aggregate deliberately merges. It therefore refines the archive's strongest result instead of diluting it with untested components.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), rank( min( ratio( apalch, at ), ratio( invch, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ConservativeDepreciationCashProfits
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, at)), RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(dpc, dp), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Among firms with equally strong pre-depreciation operating profitability, those recording heavy depreciation accruals report depressed bottom-line earnings; investors anchor on reported earnings and underprice these firms even though their cash-generating capacity, which the depreciation accrual does not touch, is identical.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the operating-liability family entirely and tests the one large non-cash accrual whose economics run opposite to working-capital accruals: depreciation lowers earnings without lowering cash, so conservatism creates an earnings-versus-cash wedge in the direction of underpricing rather than overpricing. Using EBITDA-level profitability is essential because depreciation does not enter oibdp, making the interaction a clean test of accounting conservatism rather than a mechanical decomposition of the same quantity.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( oibdp, at ) ), rank( ratio( coalesce( dpc, dp ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: SupplierCreditRegimeByProfitability
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), RANK(COALESCE(RATIO(apalch, at), RATIO(DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Expanding supplier credit means opposite things in opposite profitability regimes: for profitable firms it is negotiated financing that funds a self-sustaining operating cycle, while for unprofitable firms it is forced liquidity management that precedes distress, so the return effect of the payables flow should flip sign across the profitability distribution.
input_signals.reasoning: Centering the profitability leg makes the short leg consist of unprofitable firms that are expanding supplier credit rather than merely profitable firms with weak payables flow, which is the direct test of whether the archive's best result is a genuine interaction or a standalone payables effect riding on a profitability tilt. The tax-and-other-operating discrimination test it replaces was compromised by the undefined aoloch catch-all and by duplicating an already-flat tax leg, so this substitutes a sharper and better-measured discrimination.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_zscore( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), rank( coalesce( ratio( apalch, at ), ratio( delta( sub( lct, dlc ), 1 ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: IndustryNeutralSupplierCreditProfit
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(apalch, DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1)), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Trade-credit norms are industry-determined — retailers and wholesalers structurally run large payables while software and services run almost none — so the informative quantity is a profitable firm's payables expansion relative to its own industry's payment conventions, not relative to the whole market.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's winner ranks the payables flow cross-sectionally, which means its long leg is likely concentrated in a handful of trade-credit-intensive industries; industry-ranking the accrual leg removes that composition tilt and tests whether the alpha survives as a within-industry bargaining-power effect. If alpha holds or strengthens with more stable portfolio composition, the mechanism is firm-level supplier power; if it collapses, the archive result was an industry bet and future work should look elsewhere.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( ratio( coalesce( apalch, delta( sub( lct, dlc ), 1 ) ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: SustainedSupplierFinancingWithProfit
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), RANK(TS_SUM(RATIO(COALESCE(apalch, DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1)), at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A single year of payables expansion can be a timing artifact around fiscal year-end, but three consecutive years of cumulative supplier financing alongside high gross profitability reflects negotiated terms that suppliers have conceded permanently to a strong counterparty.
input_signals.reasoning: The five-year cumulative version bundled all three working-capital components and produced only 1.0% alpha, so this isolates the proven payables component at a shorter, coverage-preserving horizon to see whether persistence adds to or dilutes the one-year effect. Cumulating also averages out year-end payment-timing noise without imposing the five-year cash-flow-item history that cut coverage in earlier temporal signals.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), rank( ts_sum( ratio( coalesce( apalch, delta( sub( lct, dlc ), 1 ) ), at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: FreeSupplierCreditNotCostlyDebt
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), RANK(SUB(RATIO(COALESCE(apalch, DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1)), at), RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The supplier-credit premium should reflect access to *free*, non-interest-bearing financing; a profitable firm that expands payables while simultaneously drawing down short-term debt is substituting cheap for expensive capital, whereas one expanding both is simply levering up its liquidity and is not exhibiting bargaining power.
input_signals.reasoning: Netting the change in current debt against the payables flow separates negotiated trade terms from general liability expansion, which is the leading benign explanation for the archive's strongest result and one no prior signal has controlled for. It also mechanically excludes distressed firms that stretch suppliers while rolling short-term borrowings, which should clean up the short leg and improve alpha precision.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), rank( sub( ratio( coalesce( apalch, delta( sub( lct, dlc ), 1 ) ), at ), ratio( delta( dlc, 1 ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: TwoChannelAccrualCredibilityProfit
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), SUMRANK(RATIO(COALESCE(apalch, DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1)), at), RATIO(COALESCE(dpc, dp), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Supplier-financed cash generation and conservative non-cash charges are independent forms of accrual credibility — one shows profits are self-funding, the other shows profits are understated — so profitable firms exhibiting both should be the most systematically underpriced.
input_signals.reasoning: The two accrual channels with the best evidence so far use different data sources and have low economic overlap (trade terms versus fixed-asset accounting), so averaging their ranks should raise the signal-to-noise of the quality leg without narrowing coverage the way a MIN conjunction did. This is the batch's consolidation test: if the combined version beats both parents on alpha and Sharpe, later generations should build on the composite rather than on either channel alone.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), sumrank( ratio( coalesce( apalch, delta( sub( lct, dlc ), 1 ) ), at ), ratio( coalesce( dpc, dp ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: AcceleratingDepreciationConservatism
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(oibdp, at)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(COALESCE(dpc, dp), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital intensity is a slow-moving structural attribute, so a year-over-year rise in the depreciation charge per dollar of assets reflects an accounting policy shift toward shorter useful lives or faster write-offs; for firms with strong pre-depreciation profitability this conservatism depresses reported earnings without touching cash generation, and earnings-anchored investors underprice them.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the depreciation *level* with its first difference removes the capital-intensity confound that industry-ranking could not fix, because within a firm the asset base changes slowly while the charge rate reflects management's estimate choices. The interaction remains essential: rising depreciation is only an understatement-of-profit story for firms whose EBITDA-level profitability is genuinely high, and oibdp excludes depreciation so the two legs are not mechanically linked.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( oibdp, at ) ), rank( delta( ratio( coalesce( dpc, dp ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: TradeTermsBeyondPurchaseGrowth
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), RANK(SUB(RATIO(COALESCE(apalch, DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1)), at), RATIO(DELTA(cogs, 1), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Payables expand mechanically when a firm simply buys more inputs, so genuine bargaining power is payables growth in excess of purchase growth: profitable firms lengthening payment terms faster than their cost base is expanding are extracting real financing concessions from suppliers, and that advantage is durable and underpriced.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the tax-timing re-run, whose sign contradiction and sparse population would have made the result uninterpretable, and substitutes the discrimination test that actually matters for the archive's strongest signal — whether the payables premium is trade-term extension or merely a volume artifact of input growth. Both legs use well-populated income-statement and cash-flow items with a common asset scaling, so the difference is dimensionally coherent and coverage stays at the level of the existing winner.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), rank( sub( ratio( coalesce( apalch, delta( sub( lct, dlc ), 1 ) ), at ), ratio( delta( cogs, 1 ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: IndustryNeutralFreeSupplierCredit
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(SUB(RATIO(COALESCE(apalch, DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1)), at), RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Profitable firms that expand non-interest-bearing supplier financing while not increasing short-term borrowing are obtaining free capital on the strength of their franchise, and this advantage is best measured against the trade-credit conventions of their own industry rather than against the market as a whole.
input_signals.reasoning: The two independently validated improvements to the archive's core signal — netting short-term debt (alpha 4.6%, t 5.41) and industry-ranking the accrual leg (Sharpe 0.302) — address different confounds (distress-driven liability expansion versus industry composition), so combining them should compound rather than offset. This is the batch's primary consolidation candidate.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( sub( ratio( coalesce( apalch, delta( sub( lct, dlc ), 1 ) ), at ), ratio( delta( dlc, 1 ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: NegativeCashCycleProfitability
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The flow results point to a structural attribute: profitable firms that operate a negative cash conversion cycle — customers and suppliers fund the operating cycle so that net operating working capital per dollar of sales is minimal or negative — run self-financing business models whose profits require no incremental capital and are therefore more durable than the market prices.
input_signals.reasoning: Scaling net operating working capital by sales converts the stock into a cash-conversion-cycle measure in units of revenue-days, which is an operating-efficiency construct rather than the asset-scaled operating-liability leverage that was previously flagged as a Penman–Nissim rediscovery. It also tests whether the archive's flow-based finding reflects a permanent business-model characteristic or only annual payment timing, using widely populated balance-sheet items.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), sale ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: NetSupplyChainCreditPosition
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(apalch, recch), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is the firm's net position as a supply-chain financier: profitable firms that simultaneously take more credit from suppliers and extend less to customers are net borrowers within the value chain, which reflects bargaining power on both sides and frees capital, whereas firms doing the reverse are subsidizing their trading partners.
input_signals.reasoning: The payables and receivables flows have both shown strong Fama-MacBeth slopes but only payables produced FF5 alpha, so netting them into a single directional trade-credit position tests whether the receivables side adds incremental power once expressed in the same economic direction rather than as a separate quality screen. Inventory is deliberately excluded because it is a production decision, not a credit decision, and its inclusion diluted the five-year cumulative version.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( ratio( add( apalch, recch ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: SupplierCreditSurpriseVsOwnHistory
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), TS_RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(apalch, DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1)), at), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: If trade-credit expansion is informed certification, what carries information is a *change in suppliers' assessment* of the firm, which means payables growth that is unusual relative to the firm's own five-year history rather than merely high relative to other firms.
input_signals.reasoning: Every archive signal normalizes the payables flow cross-sectionally, so firms with permanently credit-intensive operating models sit in the long leg year after year; time-series ranking within the firm strips out that fixed component and tests whether the premium comes from the news content of newly extended terms. This is a different normalization axis from the industry-neutral test rather than another cross-sectional rescaling, and it directly discriminates a stable business-model interpretation from a certification-news interpretation.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ts_rank( ratio( coalesce( apalch, delta( sub( lct, dlc ), 1 ) ), at ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: PredictableProfitsWithSupplierCredit
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), NEG(VOL(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5))), IND_RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(apalch, DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1)), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Suppliers extend terms on the basis of predictability as much as level: a firm whose gross profitability is both high and stable presents low counterparty risk, so trade-credit expansion granted to such a firm is a far stronger certification of durable earnings than the same expansion granted to a firm with erratic profits.
input_signals.reasoning: Profit-level volatility is a second moment that is not collinear with the level, so unlike a three-year moving average it adds genuinely new cross-sectional information to the profitability leg rather than reproducing it with autocorrelation near 0.9. The test is economically decisive for the certification story: if adding predictability strengthens alpha, suppliers are pricing earnings reliability, whereas if it dilutes, the mechanism is simply free financing accruing to profitable firms regardless of risk.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sumrank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), neg( vol( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 5 ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( coalesce( apalch, delta( sub( lct, dlc ), 1 ) ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: LowOperatingAssetIntensityProfits
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, che), sale))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The asset side of the cash cycle carries the durability information: profitable firms that need few receivables and little inventory per dollar of sales collect quickly and turn goods fast, so their reported gross profits are already substantially realized in cash.
input_signals.reasoning: Paired with signal 3, this attributes the archive's best Fama-MacBeth result to one side of the balance sheet, which determines where the remaining generations should build. It is also the direct stock-level counterpart of the asset-side *flow* test that was priced but factor-spanned (t_alpha 0.94), so a strong result here would show that the level and the change of operating assets carry different, non-spanned information.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( sub( act, che ), sale ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: TradeCreditFundedShareOfCycle
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), SUB(act, che))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is the share of the operating cycle that trading partners fund: when operating liabilities cover a large fraction of receivables and inventory, the firm's profits are generated on capital supplied by others, and for a profitable firm this is a durable competitive position.
input_signals.reasoning: Expressing the cycle as a coverage ratio rather than a sales-scaled difference changes the cross-sectional shape substantially — it is scale-free in sales and therefore not driven by turnover differences across business models — while the denominator, non-cash current assets, is positive for essentially all operating firms so the ratio is stable. This is a distinct functional representation of the self-financing idea, not a rescaling of the difference-based construct.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( ratio( sub( lct, dlc ), sub( act, che ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ProfitsAtBestEverCycleEfficiency
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale), TS_MIN(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale), 5)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A profitable firm currently operating at or near the most working-capital-efficient point of its own five-year history has achieved a structural break in how much capital its revenue requires, and that operating improvement is more durable and less well recognized than a one-year change in working capital.
input_signals.reasoning: Distance from a five-year minimum is a nonlinear position-relative-to-own-history construct, not a first difference, so it is not the Sloan working-capital accrual with a different deflator and it does not reproduce the archive's weak accrual-change results. It also naturally filters one-year noise: a firm must beat its entire recent history, not merely last year, to score highly.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( sub( ratio( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), sale ), ts_min( ratio( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), sale ), 5 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: PredictableProfitsOnSelfFundedCycle
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), NEG(VOL(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Durable value comes from earnings that are both predictable and self-financing: a firm whose gross profitability is high and stable, and whose operating cycle requires little or no net capital per dollar of sales, generates free cash flow that the market systematically underprices.
input_signals.reasoning: This pairs the two legs with the best independent evidence in the archive — the profit-predictability leg (alpha 3.0%, t 2.93, Sharpe 0.27) and the cash-cycle leg (fmb 6.69, Sharpe 0.404) — which have never been combined, rather than smoothing an already-persistent balance-sheet ratio. Profit volatility is a second moment that is not collinear with the profitability level, so the profitability leg carries genuinely new cross-sectional information into the interaction.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sumrank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), neg( vol( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 5 ) ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), sale ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: HabitualNegativeWorkingCapitalProfits
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), RANK(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc))), 0), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Operating on a persistently negative net working capital position — customers and suppliers funding the business every single year — is a business-model characteristic rather than a balance-sheet accident, and profits generated by such a model require no reinvestment and are systematically underpriced.
input_signals.reasoning: Counting the number of years in five with a negative operating cycle is a nonlinear persistence statistic, not a moving average of the level, so it separates firms with a structural funding model from those that dipped negative once; it also censors the extreme magnitudes that make the level ratio noisy. This directly tests whether the cycle premium is about durability of the model or about the current-year magnitude.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), rank( ts_sum( indicator( neg( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ) ), 0 ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: RevenueGrowthWithoutOperatingCapital
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(SUB(GROWTH(sale, 1), GROWTH(SUB(act, che), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The self-financing advantage is most valuable when the firm is expanding: a profitable firm growing revenue faster than its receivables and inventory base is scaling without consuming capital, whereas one whose operating assets outrun sales is buying growth with credit terms and stock that will later reverse.
input_signals.reasoning: An earlier version of this idea failed construction review because it applied GROWTH to net operating working capital, a quantity that is routinely negative; both bases here — sales and non-cash current assets — are strictly positive for operating firms, so the growth differential is well defined and outlier-controlled. It tests a genuinely different aspect of the mechanism from the level tests, namely the marginal capital intensity of incremental revenue.

input_signals.name: CycleFundingRegimeByProfitability
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), SUB(act, che))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A cycle heavily funded by operating liabilities means bargaining power for a profitable firm but unpaid obligations for an unprofitable one, so the sign of the funding effect should flip across the profitability distribution rather than merely weaken.
input_signals.reasoning: Centering the profitability leg moves the short leg from "profitable firms with low trade funding" to "unprofitable firms with high trade funding", which is the state where the distress interpretation applies and where the sharpest negative returns should be concentrated. The analogous centering test on the flow leg raised the Fama-MacBeth slope from 3.56 to 4.72, so applying it to the stronger stock leg is a targeted attempt to lift the cross-sectional evidence while retaining the stock family's tradable Sharpe.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_zscore( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( ratio( sub( lct, dlc ), sub( act, che ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: CashConversionCycleInDays
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(SUB(act, che), sale), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), cogs), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The true cash conversion cycle deflates each side by its own economic driver — operating assets by revenue and operating liabilities by purchases — so a profitable firm whose customer-and-inventory days fall short of its supplier-payment days is funded by its trading partners in the literal operational sense, not merely by a favorable revenue-scaled netting.
input_signals.reasoning: Unlike a share-versus-ratio rewrite, using two different deflators produces a measure that is not a monotone transform of the archive's sales-scaled net-working-capital construct: firms with high gross margins have very different cogs and sales bases, so the cross-sectional ordering genuinely changes. Winsorizing the payables-days term controls the low-cogs service firms where that deflator is unstable, preserving coverage while fixing the one real tail problem in the family.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( sub( ratio( sub( act, che ), sale ), winsor( ratio( sub( lct, dlc ), cogs ), 1 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(che, act)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Among equally profitable firms, those whose current assets consist mostly of cash rather than of claims on customers and unsold inventory have already converted their reported profits into settled value, so their earnings require no further realization and are less prone to reversal.
input_signals.reasoning: This restores a genuine two-leg cross-theme interaction in place of the single deflator variant, and the accrual leg — the cash share of current assets — is a bounded, well-populated composition measure that has never been tested in level form, unlike the failed five-year cash-trend construction. It is also not a monotone transform of the trade-credit funding ratio, since it involves no liabilities and therefore reorders firms that fund their cycle differently.

input_signals.name: CashValidatedProfitOnShortCycle
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), RATIO(oancf, at)), IND_RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(SUB(act, che), sale), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), cogs), 1)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The profitability leg itself should be cash-validated: a firm ranking high on both gross profitability and operating cash flow generation has earnings that are simultaneously large and realized, and interacting that with a short cash conversion cycle identifies the strongest form of durable profitability.
input_signals.reasoning: Every strong archive signal uses an unmodified gross-profitability leg, so the profitability side has never been strengthened with a cash-flow channel while holding the winning accrual leg fixed — the one untested axis of the leading construct. input_signals.name: WorkingCapitalPerDollarOfProfit
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), SUB(revt, cogs)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The economically decisive quantity is how much operating capital a firm must tie up to earn a dollar of gross profit: profitable firms that generate their profits on almost no net working capital have a genuinely capital-free earnings stream, whereas the same profit financed by a large receivable and inventory book is a claim on future collection.
input_signals.reasoning: Deflating the operating cycle by gross profit rather than by sales is a cross-theme ratio — profitability enters the denominator — and it reorders firms materially because gross margins vary enormously at a given sales level, so this is not an aggregator relabeling of the days-based construct. Winsorization plus industry ranking handles the low-gross-profit tail where the ratio is unstable, and the interaction with the profitability level keeps the measure from rewarding marginally profitable firms with tiny denominators.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( winsor( ratio( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), sub( revt, cogs ) ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ProfitStreamRetainedAsCash
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(che, TS_SUM(SUB(revt, cogs), 5)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Over a five-year window, credible profits leave a cash residue: the ratio of the current cash stock to cumulative gross profit measures what fraction of the reported profit stream actually survived as settled funds, and profitable firms with a high conversion fraction have earnings that were never merely accounting entries.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the Sloan earnings-minus-cash wedge that has failed repeatedly in this archive and instead measures profit-to-cash conversion cumulatively against the profit stream itself, which is a stock-versus-cumulative-flow construct rather than a deflator swap on a published accrual measure. The denominator is a five-year sum of gross profit, so it is far more stable than any single-year accrual base, and the archive's highest-alpha leg (cash share of current assets) suggests the cash-position channel has real, non-spanned content.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( che, ts_sum( sub( revt, cogs ), 5 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: LevelAndMarginalCycleEfficiency

input_signals.hypothesis: A profitable firm can be efficient in level terms yet be buying its current growth with working capital, or vice versa; combining the standing level of the cash conversion cycle with the marginal capital intensity of this year's revenue growth identifies firms that are both structurally and incrementally self-funding.
input_signals.reasoning: Both legs independently satisfy the consolidation rule this archive has established — positive Sharpe and Fama-MacBeth slopes above 5 (cycle days 6.07/0.340; growth differential 5.41/0.369) — unlike the failed stock-plus-flow ensemble whose flow leg was factor-hedged with near-zero Sharpe. Level and marginal capital intensity are distinct moments of the operating cycle rather than algebraic restatements of one another, so the diversification of measurement error is real.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), sumrank( neg( sub( ratio( sub( act, che ), sale ), winsor( ratio( sub( lct, dlc ), cogs ), 1 ) ) ), sub( growth( sale, 1 ), growth( sub( act, che ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: CycleSignalWhereWorkingCapitalMatters
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), MUL(IND_ZSCORE(NEG(SUB(RATIO(SUB(act, che), sale), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), cogs), 1)))), IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The cash conversion cycle only carries information about profit realization when the operating cycle is a material part of the firm's balance sheet; for asset-light firms with negligible receivables, inventory and payables, an extreme cycle statistic is measurement noise rather than an economic advantage.
input_signals.reasoning: Centering the cycle leg and multiplying by a bounded materiality weight collapses immaterial-working-capital firms toward zero instead of letting them populate the extreme portfolio buckets, which is a genuine conditioning structure — the same device that lifted the Fama-MacBeth slope when applied to the flow leg — rather than a stack of correlated channels. It directly targets the most likely source of noise in the archive's best signal, so the predicted gain is in ls_talpha and Sharpe rather than in raw alpha magnitude.

input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), SUMRANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), SUB(revt, cogs)), 1)), NEG(VOL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A low working-capital requirement is only a business-model advantage if it is reliable; a profitable firm whose cycle is both light and stable can plan and distribute cash, whereas one whose working capital swings violently is exposed to periodic funding shocks that will eventually impair reported earnings.
input_signals.reasoning: Level and five-year volatility are different moments of the same operating quantity, not algebraic restatements of one another, and the analogous level-plus-volatility construction on the profitability leg previously delivered a genuine improvement in Sharpe. It also directly addresses portfolio stability, which is where the archive's leading signals still fall short of their Fama-MacBeth strength.

input_signals.hypothesis: Gross profit net of the working capital consumed to generate it is the cash the operating business actually threw off this year, and pairing that cash-adjusted profitability with a structurally light cycle identifies firms whose earnings are realized both in the current period and by design.
input_signals.reasoning: The operating-cash-flow version of this idea produced the archive's best Sharpe (0.545) but halved coverage to 0.077, so this rebuilds the cash validation from balance-sheet items available for essentially every firm, testing whether the Sharpe gain was about cash validation or about the restricted oancf sample. The profitability leg uses the annual *change* in working capital while the accrual leg uses its *level*, so the two are not mechanically redundant.

input_signals.hypothesis: A multi-year downward trend in working capital per dollar of sales reflects a deliberate operating transformation — renegotiated terms, systems investment, inventory discipline — and profits earned by a firm in the middle of such a transformation are becoming progressively more cash-backed in a way that annual snapshots understate.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has tested the level, the one-year change, the distance from a five-year minimum and the persistence count of this ratio, but never its multi-year slope, which is the natural representation of a gradual structural improvement and is far more robust to single-year window dressing than a first difference. If it delivers, the final generation can combine a level leg with a trend leg, which are different economic claims rather than restatements.

input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the averaging of two highly correlated working-capital *levels* with a marginal comparison of profit growth against operating-asset growth tests a different economic quantity — the capital cost of incremental profit rather than of installed capacity — and margin expansion enters here but not in the sales-based version already in the archive. Both growth bases are strictly positive for operating firms, so the differential is well defined and free of the sign pathology that sank an earlier growth construction.

input_signals.hypothesis: Durability is best measured by a firm's worst year, not its average one: a firm whose gross profitability never fell below a high floor across five years has demonstrated resilience, and when such earnings are also generated on minimal operating capital they are both proven and cash-realizable.
input_signals.reasoning: The five-year minimum is a downside statistic that is genuinely not collinear with the level — two firms with identical current profitability can differ sharply in their trough — so unlike a moving average this changes which firms populate the long leg, and it targets the mandate's core notion of profits that do not reverse. input_signals.name: EitherProofOfProfitRealization
input_signals.expression: MAX(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), SUB(revt, cogs)), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Exceptional standing on either dimension is sufficient evidence of durable, cash-realizable earnings — a very profitable firm with an ordinary cycle and a modestly profitable firm that ties up virtually no operating capital are both credible — so the binding evidence is the stronger of the two signals rather than their product.

input_signals.hypothesis: Operating control is revealed by how tightly working capital tracks the business: a profitable firm whose receivables, inventory and payables swing far more than its sales lacks discipline over collections and stocking, and its reported profits are hostage to periodic funding squeezes that eventually force write-downs.

input_signals.hypothesis: Two distinct disciplines make gross profit convertible into owner cash: keeping overhead small relative to the profit it supports, and keeping operating capital small relative to that same profit; a firm that consumes little of its gross profit on either dimension delivers earnings that neither the income statement nor the balance sheet claws back.
input_signals.reasoning: SG&A is the one large profitability-theme variable this entire archive has never used, and overhead intensity is economically independent of working-capital intensity — one is a cost-structure choice, the other a capital-structure-of-operations choice — so this is a new claim rather than a re-pairing of archived legs. input_signals.hypothesis: The right yardstick for capital tied up in operations is the multi-year earning power that must service it: a firm whose net operating working capital equals a small fraction of five years of accumulated gross profit has a cycle its franchise can easily carry, whereas one whose cycle rivals half a decade of profits is structurally capital-hungry regardless of this year's figures.
